prompt:
A hypothetical open-pit orogenic gold project in West Africa is at developer stage (feasibility under way). It reports 1.9 Moz at 1.5 g/t Au, free-milling, 92% recovery. An analyst lists five hypothetical candidate comparables with enterprise value (EV) per resource ounce:
A: orogenic, open pit, West Africa, developer, 2.2 Moz at 1.4 g/t, EV/oz US$85.
B: orogenic, open pit, West Africa, developer, 1.6 Moz at 1.7 g/t, EV/oz US$70.
C: high-sulphidation epithermal, open pit, Andes, developer, 2.5 Moz at 1.5 g/t, EV/oz US$140.
D: orogenic, open pit, West Africa, producer, 3.0 Moz at 1.3 g/t, EV/oz US$190.
E: orogenic, underground narrow vein, West Africa, producer, 1.0 Moz at 8.0 g/t, EV/oz US$210.
The analyst takes the median EV/oz of all five and multiplies by the target's 1.9 Moz. Which candidates would you rely on as the primary peer set, and why? Give the median EV/oz of the analyst's five and of your primary set, and the implied EV for the target on your set.
reference_answer: The analyst's median of all five (70, 85, 140, 190, 210) is US$140/oz, giving 1.9 Moz x 140 = US$266M. That set mixes deposit models, mining methods and stages. Epithermal C has different alteration, metallurgy and typical size-grade behaviour, so its multiple is not evidence for an orogenic deposit. Underground narrow-vein E has a far higher grade and a different cost and capital structure, so EV/oz is not comparable to a 1.5 g/t bulk open pit. D is the right model, method and region but a producer: producers have built plant and de-risked ramp-up, so they trade at a premium to developers; keep it as an upper-bound cross-check, not a primary peer. A and B match deposit model, method, region, stage, size and grade, so they are the primary set: median (70+85)/2 = US$77.5/oz, implied EV 1.9 x 77.5 = US$147.3M. Two peers is a thin sample, so present a range (70-85/oz, about US$133-162M) and note D as the ceiling.

rubric.criterion: Rejects epithermal candidate C because the deposit model (genesis, metallurgy, size-grade behaviour) differs from orogenic gold.
Rejects underground narrow-vein E because mining method, grade and cost structure differ from a bulk-tonnage open pit.
Identifies that producer D is not a like-for-like peer because producers trade at a premium to developers (stage mismatch), though it may be shown as an upper cross-check.
Selects A and B as the primary peer set on matching model, method, region, stage, size and grade.
Notes that two peers is a small sample and presents a range rather than a single-point value.

sources.citation: Cox, D.P. and Singer, D.A. (eds), 1986, Mineral Deposit Models, U.S. Geological Survey Bulletin 1693 (descriptive and grade-tonnage deposit models); bibliographic details seen in search results only, page not opened (HTTP 403)
JORC Code 2012 edition (Joint Ore Reserves Committee), principles on materiality and reporting of Mineral Resources; general guidance, no clause cited

review_notes: Trap: famous/convenient mixed list; median of all five looks 'robust'. Judgement call: D could be kept by some reviewers as a secondary peer; the rubric allows that. All deposits and figures invented. EV/oz basis stated as resource ounce; reviewer may want M&I vs total stated. Reviewer: numeric value set to 147.25 to match its derivation (reference rounds to 147.3). The median derivation is a hard-coded 140 because the median of five is the third sorted value.

prompt:
A hypothetical alluvial diamond project is reported at 2.4 carats per hundred tonnes (cpht) at a +1.5 mm bottom cut-off. An analyst values the in-situ resource as grade x price, using the simple average of the quoted US$/carat from four hypothetical comparable operations:
A: alluvial, +1.0 mm cut-off, 5.0 cpht, US$95/ct.
B: alluvial, +2.0 mm cut-off, 2.0 cpht, US$210/ct.
C: alluvial, +1.5 mm cut-off, 2.6 cpht, US$180/ct.
D: kimberlite pipe, +1.0 mm cut-off, 35 cpht, US$70/ct.
The analyst's value is the target's 2.4 cpht times the average of the four prices. Assess this approach and state which comparable you would lean on and what revenue per tonne you would use.
reference_answer: Analyst: average price = (95+210+180+70)/4 = US$138.75/ct; 2.4 cpht = 0.024 ct/t, so 0.024 x 138.75 = US$3.33/t. The method is unsound for three reasons. (1) Grade and price are linked by the size-frequency distribution: a finer bottom cut-off adds many small, cheap stones, raising cpht and lowering US$/ct (A: 5.0 cpht at US$95; B: 2.0 cpht at US$210). Grades and prices at different cut-offs cannot be mixed; the pair must be taken from the same cut-off. (2) D is kimberlite: different grade scale, stone population and cost base, so it should not enter an alluvial price average. (3) Price should come from a valuation of a representative parcel of the target's own stones; peers are a cross-check. The closest analogue is C (alluvial, same +1.5 mm cut-off, similar grade): 2.6 cpht x US$180 gives US$4.68/t; using the target's 2.4 cpht with C's price gives 0.024 x 180 = US$4.32/t. B and A are usable only after re-basing to a common cut-off. Revenue per tonne is the comparable metric, not cpht alone: A 4.75, B 4.20, C 4.68, D 24.50 US$/t.

rubric.criterion: Identifies that grade (cpht) and US$/ct depend on the bottom cut-off and size distribution, so they must be taken from comparables at a common cut-off.
Rejects kimberlite D as a peer for an alluvial deposit (different deposit type, grade scale and cost base).
Selects C (alluvial, same +1.5 mm cut-off, similar grade) as the closest analogue.
States that the target's own parcel valuation, not peer averages, should set the price, with peers as a cross-check.
Uses revenue per tonne (grade x price) rather than carats per hundred tonnes alone as the comparison metric.

sources.citation: Cox, D.P. and Singer, D.A. (eds), 1986, Mineral Deposit Models, U.S. Geological Survey Bulletin 1693 (descriptive and grade-tonnage deposit models); bibliographic details seen in search results only, page not opened (HTTP 403)
JORC Code 2012 edition (Joint Ore Reserves Committee), principles on materiality and reporting of Mineral Resources; general guidance, no clause cited

review_notes: Trap: averaging $/ct across cut-offs and deposit types. The analyst's error understates value, so the 'cheap' answer is wrong for the wrong reason. Judgement: using peer price for the target is a screening step only; rubric credits the parcel-valuation caveat. Numbers invented; 1 cpht = 0.01 ct/t.

prompt: A hypothetical copper project is marketed as 'a Tier-1 porphyry-style system with 350 Mt potential'. Drilling to date outlines 80 Mt at 1.1% Cu and 0.3 g/t Au. Core logging shows mineralisation as semi-massive chalcopyrite-pyrite lenses in carbonate host rocks, with garnet-pyroxene-magnetite alteration adjacent to a granodiorite stock, strongly structurally and stratigraphically controlled, with little stockwork veining. The company compares the project to the following invented, illustrative grade-tonnage model medians (not real USGS values): porphyry copper, median 100 Mt at 0.40% Cu; copper skarn, median 3 Mt at 1.7% Cu. Is the porphyry comparison appropriate? What does a grade-tonnage check say about the '350 Mt potential' claim?
reference_answer: The geological features (carbonate host, garnet-pyroxene-magnetite calc-silicate alteration at a stock contact, semi-massive sulphide lenses, strong structural and stratigraphic control, little stockwork) match a copper skarn descriptive model, not a porphyry system, so the porphyry grade-tonnage model is the wrong reference. Contained copper now: 80 Mt x 1.1% = 880 kt. Against the porphyry median (100 Mt x 0.40% = 400 kt) the target looks like a mid-sized porphyry with an unusually high grade (2.75x median), which flatters it. Against the skarn model (median 3 Mt at 1.7% = 51 kt) the 80 Mt is about 27x the median tonnage and 17x the median contained metal: already far into the upper tail of the skarn population, with a lower grade than the median (1.1% vs 1.7%), consistent with the usual size-grade trade-off. Claiming 350 Mt (3,850 kt Cu at 1.1%) would imply a deposit orders of magnitude beyond the skarn median and probably beyond anything in the model data; it requires extra evidence such as a buried porphyry source. Defensible analogues are large copper skarns (and skarn-hosted systems with an associated porphyry), assessed by size, grade and by-product gold, not Tier-1 porphyries. The claim is unsupported by the evidence presented.

rubric.criterion: Classifies the mineralisation as skarn rather than porphyry from the carbonate host, calc-silicate alteration, semi-massive lenses and structural control.
States that applying the porphyry grade-tonnage model is the wrong comparison and flatters the project's grade.
Shows the project's tonnage is roughly 27x the skarn median (or contained Cu ~17x the median), putting it in the extreme upper tail of the skarn model.
Concludes the 350 Mt potential is unsupported by the grade-tonnage model without independent evidence such as a buried porphyry system.
Mentions the size-grade trade-off: skarn grade below the skarn median at far greater tonnage is consistent with the model's inverse relationship.

sources.citation: Cox, D.P. and Singer, D.A. (eds), 1986, Mineral Deposit Models, U.S. Geological Survey Bulletin 1693 (descriptive and grade-tonnage deposit models); bibliographic details seen in search results only, page not opened (HTTP 403)

review_notes: Trap: model-type misclassification, with the wrong model making the project look mid-sized. Medians are explicitly invented; no real USGS values used. Reviewer to confirm that the geological description is unambiguous for skarn. Source verified only at search-snippet level, page not opened. Reviewer: 'probably beyond anything in the model data' is hedged; very large skarn and porphyry-skarn systems exist, so r5 (inverse size-grade trend) is a general tendency, not a rule.
